In this lesson, we'll learn how to prove some important theorems regarding the existence and number of solutions to linear congruences.

Content:
The first theorem we'll consider is a statement about the existence of a solution to a linear congruence:

Content:
> Let [MATH: a] and [MATH: b] be integers and [MATH: n] be a positive integer. If [MATH: \text{gcd}(a,n)=1], then the linear congruence [MATH: ax \equiv b \:(\text{mod}\:n)] has a solution.

Content:
To prove the theorem, we'll construct the solution to our congruence.

Content:
We start by using the conditions given in the theorem. Since these conditions involve a statement about the greatest common divisor of [MATH: a] and [MATH: n,] we can use Bézout's identity.

Content:
> Since [MATH: \text{gcd}(a,n)=1], then by Bézout's identity, there exist integers [MATH: u] and [MATH: v] such that
> [MATH: au+nv=1.]

Content:
Notice that if we write this equation modulo [MATH: n,] the second term on the left-hand side reduces to zero.

Content:
> We can write this result in modulo
> [MATH: n,] as follows:
> [MATH: au + nv|≡1|(modn); au + 0 ⋅ v|≡1|(modn); au|≡1|(modn)]

Content:
Recall that the multiplicative inverse of [MATH: a] modulo [MATH: n] is the integer such that multiplying it by [MATH: a] gives [MATH: 1] modulo [MATH: n.] So, we see that [MATH: u] fits this definition:

Content:
> This means that [MATH: u] is the multiplicative inverse of [MATH: a] (modulo [MATH: n]).

Content:
Next, we can use the multiplicative inverse to eliminate the multiplier [MATH: a] in our congruence, as shown below.

Content:
> So, multiplying both sides of the original congruence [MATH: ax \equiv b \:(\text{mod}\:n)] by [MATH: u,] we get:
> [MATH: ax|≡b|(modn); u ⋅ ax|≡u ⋅ b|(modn); (u ⋅ a)x|≡ub|(modn); 1 ⋅ x|≡ub|(modn); x|≡ub|(modn)]

Content:
This shows that a solution to the congruence exists and is given by [MATH: x_1=ub.]

Content:
Finally, we write down the conclusion.

Content:
> Therefore, the congruence has the solution [MATH: x_1 \equiv ub \: (\text{mod}\:n).]

Content:
Now that we have all of the details, let's restate the proof in full.
